row.name: West Ridge
row.overview: Alaska Grade 4 ridge combining rock, mixed ground and steep ice. Expect cornices, crevasses, serac hazard, glacier travel and tricky route finding. Skills must be solid. Mt. Hunter offers no simple escape, so plan the descent carefully.

row.name: Cassin Ridge
row.overview: A famously sought-after big-mountain line that rises along the granite spine of Denali's south side and finishes near the lower summit. What climbers now follow is a blend of later variations that sidestep a few pitches of the original ascent. Hardest single pitches come higher up, yet the long couloir near the bottom is the part most parties dread because it never lets up and sits in the path of debris dropping from above.
row.descent_text: After topping out, parties generally go down the West Buttress route.

row.name: West Ridge
row.description: The original line to the summit of the Moose's Tooth, above the Ruth Gorge. A long ridge of snow, ice and rock rather than a single technical crux, and much less travelled than the steep couloirs on the south face that draw most parties to this peak now.

row.name: West Face
row.description: The Harvard Route, put up in 1965. Steep mixed ground on one of the most striking peaks in the Alaska Range, with sustained climbing and no easy way off — the descent is as much of the undertaking as the ascent.

row.name: Hummingbird Ridge
row.description: The most serious line in the book by some distance. Climbed once, in 1965, and never repeated in its entirety: miles of corniced ridge on the biggest massif in Canada, with retreat effectively impossible once committed. It is here as a landmark of what was done, not as a route to go and do.

row.name: East Buttress
row.description: A big-wall line in the Kichatna Spires, a granite range whose weather keeps it far quieter than the Ruth. Grade VI, with aid climbing on a wall a long way from anywhere.

row.name: Northwest Arete
row.description: A knife-cut arete of quartzite rising straight above Rogers Pass. The climbing is easy for its grade and almost absurdly continuous — the appeal is the line and the exposure rather than any single hard move.

row.name: East Ridge
row.description: The classic moderate on Bugaboo Spire, taken at a friendly grade for the position it puts you in. Clean Purcell granite with a well-known gendarme pitch high on the ridge, reached from the Applebee camp above the Bugaboo Glacier.

row.name: West Buttress
row.description: The Beckey-Chouinard, and for many people the best long granite route in the range. Around two thousand feet of climbing on the far side of the Howsers, which means a committing approach over a col and a descent that is a serious part of the day.

row.name: Wishbone Arete
row.description: The highest peak in the Canadian Rockies, and a mountain notorious for turning parties back on weather rather than difficulty. The Wishbone is a long ridge of loose rock, snow and ice; the grade says little about the commitment.

row.name: North Face
row.description: A striking face above the Angel Glacier outside Jasper, and one of the most photographed walls in the Rockies. Mixed ground on typically loose Rockies limestone, best in cold, settled conditions.

row.name: Japanese Route
row.overview: Superb scenery, with a hut for the approach and the return. The rock is very loose and unpleasant, but the huge exposure and surrounding peaks make up for it.
row.description: The line of the 1925 Japanese first ascent, on a peak with a long-standing reputation as one of the hardest big summits in the Rockies to reach. Steep, loose limestone and a serious descent; the modest technical grade is not the measure of it.
